umc-001: The vulva is the external genitalia: mons pubis, labia, clitoris and vestibule. The vagina is the internal muscular canal running from the vulva to the cervix.
umc-002: The mons pubis is a pad of fatty tissue lying over the symphysis pubis, cushioning it during intercourse. Lubrication comes mainly from Bartholin's glands and the vaginal walls.
umc-003: The clitoris is part of the vulva, the external genitalia. The ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus (including the cervix) and vagina are the internal organs.
umc-004: An oocyte is an immature egg. It only becomes a mature ovum once meiosis is complete. 'Ova' is simply the plural of ovum, and 'gamete' means any sex cell, male or female.
umc-005: Each pronucleus is haploid (23 chromosomes). When they fuse, the new cell has 46 chromosomes, so it is diploid. It is called a zygote until it starts dividing; 'embryo' comes later.
umc-006: Sperm and eggs are gametes, made by meiosis, so they are haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome (X or Y in sperm). Body cells have 46.
umc-007: The fimbriae are finger-like projections at the open end of the fallopian tube. They sweep the released ovum into the tube, which carries it towards the uterus.
umc-008: Follicle growth is driven by FSH. Rising oestrogen from the dominant follicle triggers the LH surge, and it is LH that makes the oocyte complete its first meiotic division and be released. Oestrogen does not mature the oocyte itself.
umc-009: Rising oestrogen triggers a surge of LH from the anterior pituitary, and ovulation follows roughly 24 to 36 hours later.
umc-010: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH.
umc-011: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen), turning the endometrium secretory and ready for implantation. hCG is made later, by the trophoblast after implantation, and keeps the corpus luteum going.
umc-012: Red blood cells are made in red bone marrow (erythropoiesis). The cardiovascular system transports them, along with nutrients, oxygen, hormones, waste and heat.
umc-013: Perfusion is blood flowing through the capillaries of a tissue. Dilation is a vessel widening; dispersion isn't a cardiovascular term.
umc-014: The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms to the right atrium.
umc-015: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the venae cavae. Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
umc-016: The direction is reversed. The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the heart (from the left ventricle) to the body.
umc-017: Circulating blood volume rises by about 30 to 50% in pregnancy, roughly 1.5 litres. Plasma rises more than red cell mass.
umc-018: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of cells, here the heart muscle, as it adapts to the extra volume and workload. Atrophy is wasting.
umc-019: The heart enlarges to cope with the higher blood volume and cardiac output. Oestrogen is credited with stimulating growth of the heart muscle.
umc-020: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so the blood is diluted and haemoglobin concentration falls ('physiological anaemia'). Haemophilia is an inherited clotting disorder; haemochromatosis is iron overload.
umc-021: Respiration also removes carbon dioxide, and includes internal (cellular) respiration, where cells use oxygen to release energy.
umc-022: Tidal volume increases in pregnancy, by about 30 to 40%, as progesterone drives deeper breathing. Room is made by the ribcage widening and the diaphragm rising, not by smaller breaths.
umc-023: The metopic (frontal) suture lies between the two frontal bones. Sagittal: between the parietal bones. Coronal: between the frontal and parietal bones. Lambdoidal: between the parietal and occipital bones.
umc-024: The sagittal suture runs between the two parietal bones, from the anterior to the posterior fontanelle.
umc-025: In a well-flexed cephalic (vertex) presentation the denominator is the occiput. In a face presentation it is the mentum; in a brow presentation, the sinciput (frontal bone).
umc-026: The lambdoidal suture separates the parietal bones from the occipital bone, meeting the sagittal suture at the posterior fontanelle.
umc-027: The bregma is the anterior fontanelle: diamond-shaped, where the frontal, coronal and sagittal sutures meet. The posterior fontanelle is the lambda, which is triangular.
umc-028: When the head is well flexed, the suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm) presents, the smallest possible. Submentobregmatic (9.5 cm) presents in a face presentation; suboccipitofrontal (10 cm) when the head is less well flexed.
umc-029: The biparietal diameter, between the parietal eminences, is 9.5 cm. 8.2 cm is the bitemporal diameter.
umc-030: A cephalhaematoma is bleeding under the periosteum, so it can't cross suture lines and appears hours after birth. Caput succedaneum is scalp swelling above the periosteum: it crosses sutures and is present at birth.
umc-031: The sacrococcygeal joint lets the coccyx bend backwards during birth, enlarging the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet.
umc-032: The brim (inlet) is the entrance to the true pelvis; the fetus then passes through the cavity and out of the outlet. 'Inlet' and 'brim' are the same thing, so the second option makes no sense.
umc-033: The pelvic outlet is diamond (lozenge) shaped, not circular. The curve of Carus is the curved path the fetus follows through the cavity and outlet.
umc-034: The gynaecoid pelvis is the most common in women, about half. Its rounded brim is the most favourable shape for birth.
umc-035: Relaxin and progesterone soften the pelvic ligaments and joints; oestrogen increases blood supply and softening of the tissues. Adrenaline and endorphins don't affect the ligaments.
umc-036: Resistance from the pelvic floor increases flexion and makes the head rotate. The pelvic floor's forward slope then guides it round the curve of Carus, so it can extend (deflex) under the pubic arch.
umc-037: The pelvic cavity measures about 12 cm in every diameter. The inlet is widest transversely (13 cm), and the outlet is widest anteroposteriorly (13 cm).
umc-038: Pain is subjective: it is whatever the person says it is. It is shaped by emotion, culture, expectations and previous experience, not just a nervous system reaction.
umc-039: C fibres are unmyelinated, so they conduct slowly and cause a dull, aching, poorly localised pain; they respond mainly to chemical, thermal and mechanical damage. A-delta fibres are myelinated and fast, causing sharp, localised pain.
umc-040: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that detect tissue damage. Chemoreceptors detect chemicals, thermoreceptors temperature, and mechanoreceptors pressure and stretch.
umc-041: Non-painful touch, pressure and warmth stimulate large nerve fibres, which activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and 'close the gate' on pain signals. This is why massage, warm water and TENS can help in labour.
umc-042: Endorphins are the body's own opioids and rise through labour; oxytocin also has pain-relieving effects. Adrenaline and cortisol are stress hormones. The key also includes prolactin, which rises in labour, but textbooks are less clear on its role in pain relief, so check your lecture notes.
umc-043: In the latent phase the cervix changes (softens, effaces and dilates) up to 4 cm, with painful contractions. Established labour starts from 4 cm with regular painful contractions (NICE).
umc-044: Homeostasis is the body keeping its internal environment (temperature, fluid, pH, blood glucose) stable despite outside changes.
umc-045: Contractions press the presenting part onto the cervix, which triggers more oxytocin and stronger contractions (the Ferguson reflex). This loop amplifies itself until birth. Negative feedback works the opposite way, bringing a value back to its set point.
umc-046: Adrenaline and other catecholamines, released with fear or stress, inhibit oxytocin, so contractions weaken and labour can slow. This is why a calm, private environment matters.
umc-047: A full bladder can block the descent of the presenting part, reduce how well the uterus contracts, and risk bladder trauma. Women are encouraged to empty their bladder regularly in labour.
umc-048: The head descends and flexes, then rotates internally so the occiput comes to the front. It crowns and is born by extension, then restitutes, untwisting to realign with the shoulders. The shoulders rotate internally into the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet, which you see as the head turning externally. The body is born by lateral flexion.
umc-049: After the placenta separates, the interlacing muscle fibres of the myometrium contract and retract, squeezing shut the blood vessels running between them. Together with clotting, this controls bleeding at the placental site.
umc-050: A succenturiate placenta has an accessory lobe joined to the main placenta by vessels running through the membranes. If the lobe is retained, it can cause haemorrhage. Circumvallate: the membranes fold back, leaving a ring on the fetal surface. Bipartite: two roughly equal lobes.
umc-051: In a velamentous insertion, the cord inserts into the membranes and its vessels run unprotected to the placenta. Battledore: the cord inserts at the placenta's edge. Vasa praevia: unprotected vessels lie across the cervix, which can happen with a velamentous insertion.
umc-052: After birth the fundus is at about the level of the umbilicus. It descends roughly 1 cm a day, so by about a week it is halfway between the umbilicus and the symphysis pubis. It usually can't be felt abdominally after about 10 to 14 days.
umc-053: During involution, autolysis is the self-digestion of excess muscle protein by the cells' own enzymes. Ischaemia (reduced blood supply as the uterus contracts) and phagocytosis (clearing debris) are separate parts of the process.
umc-054: The key gives progesterone: pregnancy's high progesterone relaxes the vaginal walls, and as it falls after birth they regain tone and the rugae return, around three weeks after birth. Some textbooks link the rugae returning to oestrogen recovering instead, so check your lecture notes.
umc-055: In the proliferation phase, fibroblasts and new blood vessels form granulation tissue, which looks pink or red. Haemostasis is clotting, inflammation brings redness and swelling, and remodelling strengthens the scar over months.
umc-056: The frontal lobe handles reasoning, planning, problem-solving, personality and emotional expression, as well as voluntary movement.
umc-057: The temporal lobe processes hearing and smell, and is involved in memory and understanding language. The occipital lobe handles vision and the parietal lobe touch and spatial awareness. The cerebellum isn't a lobe; it coordinates movement and balance.
umc-058: The medulla oblongata, in the brainstem, contains the cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres, plus reflexes such as swallowing and vomiting. The pons helps regulate breathing; the cerebellum coordinates movement.
umc-059: Afferent (sensory) nerves carry information from the body to the brain and spinal cord. Efferent (motor) nerves carry it from the central nervous system to the body. Afferent arrives, efferent exits.
umc-060: The autonomic system controls involuntary processes such as heart rate, digestion and sweating. The somatic system controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscles.
umc-061: The sympathetic nervous system drives the 'fight or flight' response. The parasympathetic system is 'rest and digest'.
umc-062: Sodium rushes into the nerve cell (depolarisation), then potassium flows out (repolarisation). The sodium-potassium pump then restores the resting state.
umc-063: Storing minerals (calcium and phosphate) and making blood cells are metabolic functions. Mechanical functions are support and movement; protective functions include the skull and ribcage shielding organs.
umc-064: Erythropoiesis, the making of red blood cells, happens in red bone marrow.
umc-065: The alimentary canal is the continuous tube from mouth to anus: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, and small and large intestine. Accessory organs such as the liver and pancreas aren't part of it.
umc-066: Enzymes break food down chemically: lipase acts on fats, amylase on starch and trypsin on proteins. Mechanical breakdown is chewing and churning; propulsion is moving food along.
umc-067: Propulsion moves food through the tract. It starts with swallowing (voluntary), followed by peristalsis (involuntary). Chewing is mechanical digestion.
umc-068: Peristalsis is involuntary: waves of smooth muscle contraction controlled by the autonomic and enteric nervous systems.
umc-069: Ptyalism is excessive saliva. Gingivitis (gum inflammation) and epistaxis (nosebleeds) are also common in pregnancy, but they aren't about saliva.
umc-070: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, slowing the gut. Food stays longer in the colon, more water is absorbed and constipation follows. It also relaxes the cardiac sphincter, causing heartburn.
umc-071: Placental hormones increase resistance to insulin, leaving more glucose available for the fetus. If the pancreas can't make enough extra insulin, blood sugar rises: gestational diabetes.
umc-072: Gastrulation, in week 3, turns the two-layered embryonic disc into three germ layers. The name comes from the Greek for 'stomach', as it lays down the primitive gut, which is why 'formation of the gut' is the intended answer. The internal organs develop later from the germ layers.
umc-073: The three germ layers are ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Endoderm forms the lining of the gut and airways, the liver and the pancreas. Ectoderm forms skin and the nervous system; mesoderm forms muscle, bone, the heart, blood and kidneys.
umc-074: The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord, the central nervous system. Most of the peripheral nervous system comes from neural crest cells. Failure of the tube to close causes neural tube defects such as spina bifida, which folic acid helps prevent.
umc-075: The heart tube starts beating around day 22 after fertilisation, during the fourth week of development. Counted from the last menstrual period, that is about 5 to 6 weeks of gestation, so the key is using embryonic age.
umc-076: Blood flow to the kidneys rises by around half or more in pregnancy, and the glomerular filtration rate by about 50%. Waste is cleared faster, so urea and creatinine levels in the blood are lower than outside pregnancy.
umc-077: Dilated ureters and incomplete bladder emptying leave urine sitting still, where bacteria can multiply. UTIs in pregnancy can spread to the kidneys (pyelonephritis) and are linked to preterm labour.
umc-078: The medulla contains the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, which concentrate urine by reabsorbing water and salts. Urine collects in the renal pelvis and is stored in the bladder; the outer capsule protects the kidney.
umc-079: Plasma makes up about 55% of blood. Red cells make up about 45% (the haematocrit); white cells and platelets less than 1%.
umc-080: O negative red cells carry no A, B or RhD antigens, so a recipient's antibodies won't attack them. That makes O negative the universal red cell donor in emergencies.
umc-081: If a RhD-negative mother has a RhD-positive baby, fetal blood entering her circulation can make her produce anti-D antibodies. These could attack a future RhD-positive baby (haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn). Anti-D immunoglobulin, given within 72 hours of birth when the baby is RhD positive, prevents this.
umc-082: The fluid in the lymphatic system is called lymph: tissue fluid that has drained into the lymph vessels.
umc-083: The thymus is where T lymphocytes ('T' for thymus) mature and learn not to attack the body's own cells. Strictly, they start in the bone marrow and mature in the thymus. It has nothing to do with the thyroid.
umc-084: Pathogen is the umbrella term for anything that causes disease. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites are all types of pathogen.
umc-085: Diastasis recti is separation of the two rectus abdominis muscles along the midline (linea alba) as the growing uterus stretches the abdominal wall. Symphysis pubis dysfunction is pain from the pelvic joint.
umc-086: Lactogenesis is the breast developing the ability to secrete milk. Stage I begins in mid-pregnancy (colostrum); stage II, copious secretion, follows 2 to 3 days after birth as progesterone falls once the placenta is delivered. Ongoing milk production has its own name, galactopoiesis.
umc-087: Oxytocin causes the milk ejection (let-down) reflex by making the cells around the alveoli contract. Prolactin stimulates milk production.
umc-088: Milk is made by secretory cells lining the alveoli. It flows through the lactiferous ducts to the nipple. Montgomery tubercles are glands on the areola that secrete a protective, lubricating oil.
umc-089: Epigenetics is about how genes are switched on or off without changing the DNA sequence itself. Environmental factors such as diet, stress and smoking can cause these changes, including in the womb.
umc-090: Mastication is chewing: the mechanical breakdown of food in the mouth, mixing it with saliva. Swallowing is called deglutition.
